### 1. Cache Engineering for Agents (2610.28577)
- what: Proposes "cache engineering", where an agent drops selected KV entries from attention (`drop`) and re-encodes retained keys' RoPE positions (`repos`) without rewriting the text or re-prefilling, plus the AKV serving engine (extended radix tree, drop-aware eviction, segment-batch attention) to make this work behind a stateless API.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL was given for the paper itself, arXiv 2610.28577)
- key numbers: Tool-response rolling drop (keep latest 12 tool responses) vs. threshold summarization: average score +1.7 pts and cost −27.7% across 3 models × 4 benchmarks (Table 1); AKV serving at C=14 gives 1.18× output throughput and 1.51× P95 latency speedup vs. Standard on 80 SWE-bench tasks, A800 ×8 (Table 2). Table 3 shows that adding `repos` lifts BCP from 55 to 62 with tool-drop.
- code/weights: The paper states https://github.com/thu-nics/AKV. I did not check whether it resolves or what it contains.
- practical: MEDIUM
- why: The directly usable idea is the design rule that tool-response drop beats summarization on cost and score, and that drop plus repos helps once context is long. It is not practical to adopt the serving engine, since it needs SGLang changes, a custom radix tree and segment-batch attention, and the paper's baselines are self-run and single-harness, not my Claude/Muninn setup. Also, the API `cache` field is only a proposal; no hosted API exposes it, so the Muninn analogue would be a harness-level "drop old tool results" policy, not a KV operation.

### 1. LiFT: Loop Flow Transformers (2610.05538)
- what: Trains a looped DiT core where each loop is supervised at a point on a straight path from the initial velocity estimate to the flow-matching target, so loop count can be raised at inference without retraining.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL was given for the paper itself, so I rated from the supplied text only)
- key numbers: L/2 R10 with 2 training loops goes from FID 20.30 to 10.95 at 8 inference loops (50 steps); it reaches 12.25 at 4 loops and 14.79 TFLOPs, against dense L/2 at 16.94 with 8.07 TFLOPs at 50 steps and dense XL/2 at 14.69 with 23.72 TFLOPs. Parameters are 270M against 675M for XL/2.
- code/weights: not stated ("Coming Soon" placeholders appear in the abstract area; no repository or checkpoint link in the text)
- practical: LOW
- why: The setting is class-conditional ImageNet 256 with a DiT-scale model trained for 500k updates on 4 H100s and no classifier-free guidance, so replicating it means training a DiT, not just running a tool. No code or weights are released, and the authors note that each result is a single run. The one transferable idea is that more loops at inference can buy quality, and that is directly relevant to your model-routing thinking, but it does not change a design decision you can make this month.

### 1. Embodied Turing Machines: Stateful Code for Robot Recursive Self-Improvement (2610.12369)
- what: Proposes Code-Only-as-Policy (COAP), a frozen, model-free code library that tracks robot and environment state with perception code, with coding agents improving it offline; evaluated on the 42-task RoboDojo benchmark in simulation.
- read: full (text supplied in the review request; no URL was given in the input, so I rated from the pasted text only)
- key numbers: 70.24% overall SR vs 31.38% for the best leaderboard entry (PhysicalRSI, agent+VLA) and 27.96% for the best VLA; Memory 89.9% and Precision 75.1%. The paper's own Figure 5 shows 63% SR on measured state vs 83% on oracle state, so the headline depends on the simulator's public camera, mesh, and object-size constants.
- code/weights: not stated (the paper mentions no repository, released library, or weights)
- practical: LOW
- why: The result is simulation-only, and the paper says its perception relies on benchmark constants (camera parameters, robot meshes, object sizes) that would need re-measuring on a real robot. Its main practical lesson for you is the design pattern (explicit state in code, a frozen policy, default-off parameters for backward-compatible extensions, and per-decision branching with acceptance gates), which is worth borrowing for Muninn's skills and routing rules even though the robotics results won't transfer directly. The authors also acknowledge that all 40-task merges were selected on validation, and the paper provides no seeds-level variance beyond the 3×50 layouts per task.

### 1. Harness^2: Recursive Agent Harnessing for an Open World (2610.14224)
- what: Proposes a recursive harness-optimization loop, with a contrastive Propose–Probe–Compose step for per-task harness edits (no ground-truth verifier) and an updated "improvement harness" library that carries lessons across a task stream.
- read: full (text supplied in the request; no URL was used to fetch it)
- key numbers: One step lifts GLM-5 on WorkBuddy-Bench Avg. from 64.2 to 75.7 under OpenCode (+11.5), and Gemini 3.5 Flash from 72.4 to 77.5 (+5.1); k=5 parallel recursion adds a further 2.9–3.9 points. Harness Scaling underperforms the base in 7 of 12 pairs. Ablations (Table 3) remove 1.6–3.7 points each, from n=3 runs with large std (often 2–5).
- code/weights: github.com/google-research/harness2 and harness2.github.io are stated in the paper. No model weights.
- practical: MEDIUM
- why: The concrete, reusable pieces are the on-disk component layout (system prompt, guardrails, memory, skills, subagents, scripts, plugin), the trigger-line and no-template-brace validation rules, and the "a skill exists only once named in always-on text" constraint, all of which you could copy into Muninn's harness. ### 1. Next-Concept Modeling: Fast, Parallel Coarse-to-Fine Text Generation (2610.14162)
- what: Trains a multiscale residual VQ-VAE to turn text into a coarse-to-fine hierarchy of discrete codes, then a ~100M transformer generates each level in parallel, so generation takes K≪L steps instead of denoising the full sequence.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL was provided, the paper's own text is the source)
- key numbers: LM1B Gen. PPL 93.05 at 12 NFE vs DUO 97.30 at 128 NFE (Table 8), and 21× faster wall-clock. XSum ROUGE-L 28.0 at 8 NFE vs AURORA-LM 26.6 at 128 NFE (Table 2). Sudoku Hard 86.1% vs FMLM+ 81.3% (Table 3).
- code/weights: GitHub link stated (https://github.com/HazyResearch/ncm); weights not explicitly stated.
- practical: MEDIUM
- why: The recipe is a concrete design pattern (residual VQ hierarchy plus next-scale generation, with block-diagonal attention and code corruption) that a builder could replicate on small text tasks, and the released code makes that feasible. The headline speedups rest on single-GPU H100 timings, fixed ~100M models, and a fixed level schedule, and the 21×/31× comparisons are against diffusion baselines that were not tuned for wall-clock. Nothing here touches Muninn's routing or memory layer directly, so it is a watch item for in-browser small-model inference rather than something to adopt now.

### 1. TokenRouter: Efficient Serving System for Token-Level LLM Routing (2610.12242)
- what: Proposes a serving runtime for token-level LLM routing (SGLang-based), with per-model subservers, a route-send-receive programming interface, handoff-resume for routed requests, and a delayed-batching scheduler whose threshold is chosen from a DTMC throughput model.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL fetched, rated from the supplied paper text)
- key numbers: 2.01–64.15× decoding throughput over existing implementations (abstract, across 15 algorithm–workload combinations); vs. SGLang-based Std. Serving at concurrency 4, Table 2 gives R2R 244.56 vs 89.62 tok/s (official) and CITER 149.31 vs 17.16 tok/s; ablation at N=8 shows R2R official 134.89 vs TokenRouter 372.48 tok/s (~2.76×), with delayed batching adding 1.26× over async (Table 6).
- code/weights: GitHub link stated in abstract (https://github.com/thu-nics/TokenRouter); no weights released or stated.
- practical: MEDIUM
- why: The serving-side ideas (handoff-resume that keeps prefix/KV state across model switches, and the in-process router to avoid IPC per token) are transferable to any multi-model local setup, and the code is public. Practical adoption is limited, though: the gains come from a ~2 GPU, 8×A100 setup with SGLang 0.5.1, the headline 64× figure is against the weakest baseline, and the delayed-batching gain only shows up at higher concurrency. The paper's own tables show the advantage shrinking at N=1 (Table 5, about 1.9–10× vs official code). Your use case, a cheap model delegating to a larger one per token, is not a common deployment pattern for an agent's cost routing, so the value is mostly as a reference design rather than something to drop in.

### 1. Vela: User Behavior as Supervision Sparks LLM Intelligence (2610.14709)
- what: Converts 100k anonymized social-platform user behavior histories into 75k SFT tasks (Predictive + Rubric questions with rule- and rubric-based scoring), fine-tunes Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on them, and reports gains on in-domain, user-OOD and general benchmarks.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL fetched, paper text taken as given)
- key numbers: VelaBench 51.5 → 63.0 (+11.5) for Vela-35B-A3B vs base; general OOD average 54.2 → 58.2 (+4.0), with GPQA-Diamond +4.6 and AIME 2026 +0.8; RL from the SFT checkpoint reaches 66.2 vs 58.5 from base on VelaBench. The Vela-RFT variant (self-generated trajectories, 9,375 samples) gains only +2.0 in-domain and holds the general average flat.
- code/weights: GitHub link stated (https://github.com/AllSpark-Research/Vela) and the authors say they "will publicly release" templates, prompts and training/eval code; no weights release stated. The composer and scorer are Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B, a 2.4T model, so the pipeline is not cheap to reproduce.
- practical: LOW
- why: The main claim rests on a single base model, a 2-epoch SFT run, and a benchmark (VelaBench) built by the same pipeline that generated the training tasks, so in-domain gains are partly self-referential. Reproducing the data generation needs a 2.4T scorer and access to a private platform behavior corpus, which a weeks-scale replication cannot match. The one transferable idea is the design choice of filtering tasks to mean-score [0.2, 0.8] (ablation +1.1 user-OOD average, no in-domain change) and the leak-avoidance rule of never pairing Predictive and Attribution questions on the same future event; that is a useful pattern for building eval sets for a memory or routing agent, but it does not change a design decision on its own.

- what: Introduces a 50-task, executable, multi-turn benchmark of payments-company business workflows (789 documents, 601 discoverable tools, simulated customer) that scores goal attainment, process compliance, and protection compliance deterministically over execution histories, not just final state.

- what: Introduces a 50-task, executable, multi-turn benchmark of payments-company business workflows (789 documents, 601 discoverable tools, simulated customer) that scores goal attainment, process compliance, and protection compliance deterministically over execution histories, not just final state.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL fetched, and the supplied text is the only source used)
- key numbers: Claude Opus 5 strict success 64.0% (1 run/task); DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash goal 46.7% vs strict 43.3%, and 191.3 assistant tool calls per run vs 111.8 in Golden traces (1.71x); "no cap" 43.3% vs 1.5x-Golden-call cap 6.7%.
- code/weights: GitHub https://github.com/ant-intl/BizBench and Hugging Face dataset https://huggingface.co/datasets/ant-intl/BizBench are stated in the paper.
- practical: MEDIUM
- why: The most transferable pieces are the evaluation design (split goal/process/protection checks, replay of a Golden trace to prove feasibility, and a call-budget ablation) and the finding that a single-run success metric hides reserve-breach and approval-order violations. This applies directly to a Muninn-style agent that delegates to cheaper models, since it argues for gating tool calls and auditing intermediate state, not just final output. It is not a model or routing result, though: the benchmark is a fixed 50-task set with a payments-specific environment and only three runs for most models, so I would not treat its absolute rankings as a routing signal without rerunning on my own workflows.

### 1. Training Foundation Models with a Single Algorithm (2610.40564)
- what: Reframes pretraining, midtraining, SFT and binary-reward RL (MaxRL/REINFORCE/TailRL) as weighted maximum-likelihood fits to mixtures of static data and model-generated success-conditioned samples, and trains them in one asynchronous trainer.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL fetched)
- key numbers: Controlled 124M-parameter reasoning-puzzle study: best unified config reaches higher Base/Extended accuracy than the best staged config (Fig. 4; staged reference pass@1 24.54 Base, 16.91 Extended, Table 9). Real-world 0.76B math study: unified 0% mixing matches staged RL on math (Math pass@1 24.75 vs 24.16) while running 7.8x faster per update (3.7s vs 28.8s, App. D.6). Retention: pretraining loss at 2.537–2.540 for unified vs 12.1–15.1 for staged midtraining at 2e-4 (Table 11).
- code/weights: Website, GitHub (github.com/yudasong/unified-training) and Hugging Face (huggingface.co/sfanm/unified-training) links are stated in the abstract.
- practical: MEDIUM
- why: The most transferable result is the recipe itself: a single weighted-CE loss over a buffer mixing static data and RL samples weighted 1/p̂ on correct completions (Eq. 2, Sec. 4.2), plus the finding that mixing a small slice of reasoning or midtraining data into RL reduces forgetting far more than a KL penalty does (App. E). Skepticism: all experiments are small (124M and 0.76B models), most RL runs use one seed-pair, the staged baselines were tuned on the same metric, and the paper concedes it gives no predictive mixture-selection rule, so it changes design thinking more than it gives a drop-in recipe.

### 1. PDRVLA: A Vision-Language-Action Model with Physical Dynamics Representations (2610.37381)
- what: Adds a 57M-parameter Physical Dynamics Module that reads intermediate VLM features (layer 8) and emits 50 physical tokens, trained by direct prediction of future RGB/depth/flow VAE latents plus a frozen LingBot-Video world model, then used as extra conditioning for a flow-matching action expert with no video generation at control time.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL given beyond the arXiv id 2610.37381)
- key numbers: Ablation on held-out RoboCOIN clips: mean normalized future-feature MSE 0.6439 to 0.6354 (1.32% reduction) with world-model assistance; the flow gain is 0.62% with an interval including zero. Benchmarks: LIBERO 99.3 vs Qwen-RobotManip 99.1; LIBERO-Plus 89.9 vs 89.0; RoboTwin 2.0 93.6 vs 93.2; SimplerEnv 81.5 vs 80.8. Subtask conditioning on LIBERO-Plus moves 89.93 to 90.23, and ECoT generation at inference gives no consistent gain.
- code/weights: not stated
- practical: LOW
- why: The headline gains over baselines are 0.2 to 1.1 points, and the paper reports single-seed numbers with no variance, so they are hard to separate from noise. ### 1. Recursive Self-Improvement through Multi-Agent Self-Supervision (MASS) (2610.12176)
- what: Alternates an inner loop where one model, playing executor, evaluator and optimizer, evolves multi-agent orchestrator/subagent workflow prompts, with an outer loop that SFTs the same model on the selected multi-agent trajectories, then repeats for two cycles on Qwen3.6-27B.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL fetched, paper text is the source) 
- key numbers: Public-benchmark score per output token 1.2–1.6× the base on four research benchmarks; test-task win rate vs base 53.9% (cycle 1) → 69.9% (cycle 2); a single-agent student gets 64.0% at ~1.4× the tokens vs 68.3% for the multi-agent student. Terminal-Bench 2.0 (37.5→35.2) and SWE-bench Verified (62.6→61.1) do not improve, and the paper's own significance tests on MLR-Bench are mostly non-significant on paired tests (p=0.23–0.55).
- code/weights: code https://github.com/SakanaAI/mass and blog https://pub.sakana.ai/mass/ stated in the paper; no weights release stated.
- practical: MEDIUM
- why: The reusable parts are the workflow-as-prompt orchestrator/subagent format, the observation that contracts and hops carry the task-specific information, and the "delegation + code handoff" audit as a way to check that a model actually coordinates. Adopting the full loop needs an 8-task private benchmark, GPT-5.5/Opus judges and ~19 GPU-hours of SFT, which is out of reach for a weeks-long test, and the gains are on a single model with a judge that the paper itself calls non-independent.

### 1. Thinking Inertia: LLMs Keep Thinking When Told Not To (arXiv 2610.11765)
- what: Defines no-thinking as a response-level property (empty pre-answer text, question relevance, LLM-judged explicit inference) and measures six prompt/template interventions across six LLMs on Bool, MCQ and open-ended math/QA tasks.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL was given for the paper itself, so I rated from the supplied text only)
- key numbers: Open-ended, M2 (native Think-Off) EIR 99.69%; M5 (strict "answer directly") EIR 62.00% with ETR rising to about 40% and accuracy down about 15 points. Bool M2 EIR 5.15% vs MCQ 45.57%. Judge agreement: GPT-5.5 vs Claude Opus 4.8 binary 97.3% overall; human vs GPT-5.5 binary 98.8%.
- code/weights: no code or artifact link stated in the supplied text; the paper mentions "evaluation artifacts" and per-example annotations but gives no URL.
- practical: MEDIUM
- why: The useful, changeable finding is that "no-think" flags and "answer only" instructions don't remove visible reasoning, so a router that trusts `enable_thinking=false` or a short output as a cheap-model signal will misclassify. Answer-space is a strong predictor: Bool and candidate-visible formats compress easily, open generation does not, so that belongs in the routing rule. The evaluation is on 2026 frontier models with deterministic decoding and a GPT-5.5 judge, so the specific rates won't transfer directly to your stack, and replicating the full EIR pipeline needs a judge model you may not have access to.

### 1. RSI-Anything: Unlocking Recursive Self-Improvement with World Models (arXiv 2610.13912)
- what: Proposes a framework that uses a JEPA-style world model to rank candidate actions before costly external execution, adapts the world model from feedback when reliability checks trigger, and retains policy–model pairs only if component and pair checks pass, evaluated across code repair, GUI, lab planning, reaction optimization, and an immune-science case.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL fetched) — the supplied text is the paper's own body, method, and tables.
- key numbers: Code repair with the coder fixed: 26.3% static verifier → 29.2% fixed world-model selection → 31.2% with world-model adaptation (200 CodeContests tasks, 3 seeds, 4 candidates/round, 3.72 online test calls/task). Reaction optimization: 96.15% vs 82.16% for Bayesian optimization at 40 experiments in a single flow LC–MS screen. GUI checkbox: 51% → 99% success, mean actions 5.30 → 3.21.
- code/weights: Repo link https://github.com/Gen-Verse/RSI-Anything and a Hugging Face link are stated on the paper's front page. The HF link is labelled "Models" but points to a `datasets/` path, so it is unclear whether weights are released. Whether the W1 world model or the ReactionT5 adapter is included is not stated.
- practical: LOW
- why: The most transferable idea is ranking four candidate fixes with a cheap predictor of execution-class probabilities before running the expensive check, which is directly relevant to routing and gating. However, the reported gains are small (2.8 pp over a static verifier, CI [+0.17, +5.50]), come from one coder and one benchmark family, and the "recursive" loop is only shown across successive cycles in some domains, not as joint multi-round training, which the authors admit in the Discussion. The reaction result rests on a single screen at 40 experiments, with no seed or variance reported.

### 1. The Trinity: Capability-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Multimodal Agents (arXiv 2610.36077)
- what: Builds a capability tree from training-task trajectories, uses an LLM "Creator" to generate simplified training worlds per node, evolves per-node Harness modules ("Explorer") that are selectively inherited down the tree, and routes tasks to one of the resulting Harnesses with an agent-router that reads capability cards and retrieved past outcomes. Backbone is a frozen Claude Opus 5.
- read: full (text supplied in the request; not fetched from arxiv.org/abs/2610.36077 or the project page)
- key numbers: Train mean 39.06 (Base) → 73.16 (Iter 4); Unseen mean 37.45 → 63.61. Module-only ablation on same benchmarks: Global 53.04/42.92 vs Capability Tree (Sim) 56.95/47.26. Self-routing with capability cards and memory reaches 71.27/60.96 against an Oracle of 73.16/63.61. Benchmark-level gains are large but partly from benchmarks the authors built or rebuilt themselves.
- code/weights: GitHub https://github.com/InfRec-Cardinal/The-Trinity and project page https://trinity-rsi.github.io/ are stated. Model weights are not applicable (frozen closed backbone).
- practical: MEDIUM
- why: The routing result is the transferable piece: a per-task agent router that reads capability descriptions and verified outcome memory, with a FIFO memory and a cosine ≥0.5 retrieval threshold, is something he could copy into Muninn's subagent routing within weeks. The headline RSI numbers rest on a frozen Opus 5 backbone with evolved scaffolding, a large environment-generation pipeline, and benchmarks the authors rebuilt from web sources, so they are hard to reproduce cheaply and are not evidence that a small model plus external KB matches a large one.

- what: Replaces the DRAM-then-SSD tiered KV-cache hierarchy with a flat design where DRAM and NVMe SSD are peer media behind a 64-bit address space, places each session's KV blocks once at write time in layer-major contiguous SSD extents, and streams coalesced reads into a bounded GPU window via GPUDirect Storage, implemented in SGLang.
- read: full (text supplied in the request; no URL given in the paper text beyond the arXiv id)
- key numbers: On a Claude Code trace with DeepSeek-V4-Flash at 1.0 QPS, mean TTFT 7.57 s vs. 12.24 s for Mooncake (1.6x) and 17.51 s for host-DRAM-only; delivered hit rate 94.2–94.6% vs. Mooncake's 64.3% under load; SSD read amplification 6.5–6.7x lower than Mooncake. On Llama-3.1-70B at 64K, TTFT 3.74 s vs. Mooncake-GDS 6.60 s, but Mooncake-GDS matches FlatCake at 16K (2.31 vs 2.32 s).
- code/weights: not stated in the paper text. The paper says it is implemented in SGLang v0.5.19 with about 8.8K lines of C++/CUDA and 7.1K lines of Python, but gives no repository link.
- practical: LOW
- why: The mechanisms need a GDS-capable NVMe RAID, 8×B200 or A100 class GPUs, and a SGLang fork with no released code, so a weeks-long replication is unrealistic. The transferable idea is narrower: write-once, session-contiguous, layer-major placement, which is a design choice a KV-offload team could apply. The headline gains are against Mooncake on a single production trace under a tuned testbed, and the paper's own Mooncake-GDS comparison shows the advantage shrinks at short contexts.

### 1. Learning the 4D World through Point Trajectory Forecasting (2610.28594)
- what: Video-Point Model (VPM), a multi-view video world model built on Cosmos3-Nano that jointly generates future multi-view video and 3D point trajectories via a trajectory head plus a cross-view correspondence loss, with an optional action-token branch for robot control.
- read: full (text supplied in the prompt; no URL was fetched, paper text taken as given)
- key numbers: On VP-WorldBench Sim Robot, FVD 104.74 (Cosmos3-Nano) → 78.52 (VPM V) → 67.35 (VPM V+T); δ3D_avg 39.03 → 43.62 → 50.05. On real-world Robot, the real-robot success rate on the PnP Cube task is 54.2% for VPM (V+T+A) vs 43.8% for VPM (V+A) (hard task, 24 trials, half-credit scoring).
- code/weights: Project page and Hugging Face datasets (VPM-Data, VP-WorldBench) are linked. No model weights or training code link is stated in the paper text.
- practical: LOW
- why: The core method needs 32 GH200 GPUs and a 600K-sample mixed corpus, so the gains are not reproducible on a laptop-scale budget. The released benchmark and the cross-view MEt3R fix are usable, but there are no weights stated, and the paper's own ablation shows the gains are conditional on the trajectory head and its three-stage curriculum. The one transferable finding is that dense point-track supervision beat per-frame depth/pointmap supervision in its Table 22, which is worth keeping in mind for any future geometry-aux training of small video or world models.

### 1. You don't need long context (2611.05306)
- what: Evaluates "end-of-conversation compaction" and "single-action compaction" on long-horizon and long-input agent benchmarks, arguing that frontier models keep accuracy while living in 16K–48K contexts, and proposes "semantic state space models" as a post-training target.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL fetched, paper text taken as given)
- key numbers: Opus 4.5 on SWE-bench Verified: 70.0% baseline vs 74.8% best EoCC (48K/36K) and 70.2% under single-action compaction, with median peak context 8–9K vs 32K baseline median. Cost multiples on long-horizon tasks 2.2x–8.8x (Opus) using the paper's own estimated optimized retail cost, which rests on a 0.20 cost-ratio taken from throughput measurements on three open-weight models served on H100s, and a made-up 5:1 output-to-input and 10:1 cached-input pricing scheme. Long-input tasks: RULER 62.5% → 95.7% for Opus at 16K.
- code/weights: Project Moonshot link (research.nvidia.com/labs/lpr/lfi/) and lab link are stated; no code or harness release is stated in the text supplied.
- practical: MEDIUM
- why: The compaction prompt templates (Appendix G) and the "carefully cherry-picked brief" structure (verbatim task, current intentions, plan, artifacts, requirements) are copyable this week and map directly onto Muninn's boot-context and handoff design. The cost multiples are the weak part: they depend on an estimated pricing formula rather than published prices, so treat the 2–9x figure as an upper-bound sketch, not a billing fact. Frontier-model-only results and the paper's own note of a 3.6K→ catastrophic Qwen 3 Coder Next collapse (3.6% at 16K) mean the headroom is model-specific and needs your own eval before you move a routing threshold.

### 1. Learning from Fleet Experience: A Collective Learning Paradigm for Robots (2610.25736)
- what: Introduces collective experience learning (CEL) and FERT, which retrieves successful fleet trajectory segments using failure contexts (S-DTW over visual+proprioceptive embeddings) and fine-tunes a pi0 VLA on them, plus FATS, a fault-tolerant async training system for 96 robots.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL given beyond the project page cel-robot-learning.github.io, which I did not open). The text supplied is the full paper body, appendices included.
- key numbers: Phone Packaging 79.2% → 98.3% with 96 robots; 16-robot ablation removing failure-guided retrieval drops 86.7% → 64.2%; 5-task average (M)HG-DAgger 81.0% → FERT 97.3%. Baselines are RLT (75.8% on Phone Charging) and RECAP (75.0% on Phone Packaging), both with human corrections, so the comparison is not matched on supervision.
- code/weights: not stated in the paper text (project page only; no repo or checkpoint link in the body).
- practical: LOW
- why: The method needs a 96-robot-scale physical fleet, six A800 servers, and a RLinf-based async stack, so it is not replicable within weeks. The one transferable idea is the failure-query → DTW-retrieval → priority-weighted sampling pattern over a success buffer, which could be tried offline on existing episode logs with a small embedding model, but the paper gives no evidence that it works without the physical loop. Note the stated theory (Lemma 2, Theorem 1) only covers a single first-order update, and the ablation uses one seed-free configuration per setting with two held-out robots, so the reported gains carry noticeable uncertainty.

### 1. ThinkWorld: World Imagination Reinforces Chain-of-Dynamics Reasoning (2610.37666)
- what: Trains a Qwen3-VL-2B VLA to emit discrete FAST-tokenized "Chain-of-Dynamics" motion tokens, then uses GRPO with a DINO-feature agreement reward (predicted vs observed 1s-ahead frame) so unlabeled human/robot videos can refine the reasoning.
- read: full (text supplied in the prompt; no arXiv URL was fetched separately, the paper's own project page is https://thinkworld-project.github.io/)
- key numbers: LIBERO-PRO avg 55.6% vs VLA-JEPA 48.5% (reproduced) and pi0.5 53.2%; real-robot macro SR 94.4% vs MolmoAct2 62.2%; RL adds only +1.2 pts over the CoD+future-prediction stage (54.4 to 55.6), from a single training seed.
- code/weights: not stated (project page only; no repo or checkpoint link in the text).
- practical: LOW
- why: The method needs 128+64 H100s for SFT and RL on a 390M-frame corpus, and the released artifacts are unknown, so nothing here is adoptable within weeks. The reusable ideas are narrow: the "reward a reasoning trace by how well its imagined future matches the observed future" pattern and the motion-weighted DINO similarity, both of which are cheap to test on your own video data, but the paper's own ablation shows the RL step itself contributes only about one point, from one seed, so I'd treat the gain as unproven.

- what: Introduces a 56-task benchmark of end-to-end physics research tasks written by 42 physicists from their own projects, graded by deterministic verifiers plus rubric-based reviewer agents with blocker and non-blocker criteria, and evaluates 22 models across 26 configurations.

### 1. VFlash: Fast, Accurate Visual Planning via Flash Primitive Decoding (2611.08449)
- what: Trains a small non-causal diffusion drafter on a frozen 4B VLM to predict an entire visual primitive (box, 2D/3D trajectory, dense point motion) in one pass, and accepts schema-valid blocks without token-level agreement with the autoregressive target.
- read: full (text supplied in the prompt; no URL was given for the paper itself, the GitHub and project links are the authors' own) — the appendices with the per-task budgets, latency tables and protocols were all included, so I rated from the full text.
- key numbers: Table 4 3D trajectories: ADE on AgiBot drops from 0.105 (AR, 2D+3D) to 0.041 (VFlash), and SR@5 rises from 0.398 to 0.739. Table 3 boxes: 2.6–2.8× BPS over AR with AR fallback, but direct (no fallback) mean F1 falls from 60.1 to 39.1 on Dense200. Table 7 MolmoSpaces: 62.6% baseline → 70.2% with VFlash plans, against 61.0% for AR-generated plans.
- code/weights: the paper lists a GitHub link (https://github.com/NVlabs/Eagle/tree/main/Embodied) and a project page (https://research.nvidia.com/labs/lpr/vflash/). It does not clearly say whether the drafter weights are released; the MolmoMotion-AR target it builds on is released by its authors. I could not verify the repo contents from the supplied text.
- practical: MEDIUM
- why: The core idea is portable to your own stack: a small drafter trained on frozen-model features, with a schema-driven block length and a structural validator in place of target-token verification. The reported speedups come from NVIDIA's own TensorRT-Edge-LLM build on Jetson Thor, DGX Spark and H100, and the 25× dense-motion figure is single-rollout only, so treat both as unverified until you measure them yourself. Table 3 also shows direct acceptance without a fallback loses a lot of accuracy on crowded scenes, so the fallback guard is not optional.

### 1. Agentic Backdoors via Pretraining Poisoning (arXiv 2610.37741)
- what: Shows that poisoning 0.1% or less of a 100B-token FineWeb pretraining corpus with declaration-style or demonstration-style documents implants a remote-code-execution backdoor (`curl ... | bash`) that survives SFT, DPO and GRPO into a Qwen3-based CLI agent, with ASR rising with model size.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL fetched)
- key numbers: 4B declaration-based model with ordinary-string `anthropic` path trigger reaches 92.7% Pass@32 ASR after GRPO (vs. 0.0% on clean NL2SH-ALFA prompts and ≤0.06% on trigger-free prompts); rare-string trigger reaches 10.5% at 4B, 4.0% at 1.7B, 2.1% at 0.6B; at 0.0005% poison (~2,500 documents) the 4B model still fires on 1.4% of prompts (single seed).
- code/weights: code at https://github.com/safety-research/agentic-backdoor (stated in abstract). No model weights stated.
- practical: LOW
- why: The threat is real and the trigger finding matters for design, but the attack needs a from-scratch pretraining budget (100B tokens, 8–16 H200s per run), so you cannot replicate it within weeks. The actionable takeaway is defensive: treat the provenance of any retrieved or ingested web content, and the agent's action layer, as part of the security model. Your Muninn setup already has the right instinct by gating the command path and not trusting ambient text, but nothing here changes a routing or memory design decision directly.

### 1. Memorilla: Latent Semantic Memory for LLMs (2610.21375)
- what: Trains a small cross-attention memory module that reads frozen document embeddings and emits 16 query-conditioned soft tokens injected into a frozen Qwen3-8B's input embedding space, with no decoder changes.
- read: full (text supplied in the prompt; no URL fetched, paper's own text used) 
- key numbers: FactKG 84.33% vs 80.43% full context (108x fewer doc tokens); LaMP-4 ROUGE-L 18.15 vs 14.21 full context; TextWorld avg@3 0.242 vs 0.186 full-history ICL (pass@3 0.375 vs 0.250), with only 8 latents there.
- code/weights: Paper says code, training/eval data with precomputed embeddings, and PV4 data are released at https://memory.stanford.edu/ (release status not independently verified).
- practical: MEDIUM
- why: The design (frozen embedder + small trainable reader + frozen decoder, 16 soft tokens, store reusable across queries) is directly relevant to a Muninn-style external memory, and the TextWorld result is a concrete agent-memory signal. However, every headline gain needs roughly 2M+1.3M training examples and GRPO on a 4B agent, and the paper itself concedes the memory loses fine-grained facts and that RAG wins on exact-entity questions (NarrativeQA who/which, PubMedQA where LLMLingua-2 leads), so a hybrid with retrieval is the realistic design takeaway rather than a drop-in replacement.

### 1. Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety (2611.08438)
- what: A survey of mechanistic interpretability for AI safety that covers SAEs, transcoders/CLTs, circuits, probing, steering, learning dynamics and training-data attribution, and proposes an evaluation framework and six research orientations.
- read: full (text supplied in the prompt; the arXiv URL is https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08438, and the paper's own notebook and website links are in its abstract). I read the text through Section 6.10.4, and the supplied text is truncated before Sections 7–14.
- key numbers: Top-k SAEs commonly use k=32 to 150 (Gao et al., 2025; Karvonen et al., 2025). Batch Top-k and JumpReLU are the reported reconstruction leaders at matched sparsity. Dead features can reach 10–50% of a poorly tuned dictionary, and fewer than 50% of features may match across seeds. CLT top-1 agreement on a full replacement model is about 50% on Pile prompts, on an 18-layer model. Training a CLT suite for Gemma-2-9B took about 3,844 H100-hours.
- code/weights: Notebooks at https://github.com/TSGLAB/Interpretability_Survey_Safety and website https://tsglab.github.io/mi_survey/. The paper points to Gemma Scope, Llama Scope and Neuronpedia for released SAE weights.
- practical: MEDIUM
- why: The survey is mostly a map, but it gives useful SAE design guidance: Top-k at k≈32 for a cheap start, report dead-feature rate and seed stability, and validate features with necessity/sufficiency/specificity tests. Its own claims still depend on sections I could not see, so the Section 7–14 evaluation framework and safety-application findings remain unrated.

### 1. SLA: Scaling Spatial-Language-Action Model via Continual Pre-training (2611.08373)
- what: Continual-pretrains a pi0.5 VLA with an auxiliary loss that aligns intermediate visual tokens (gated multi-layer fusion) to frozen OmniVGGT 3D features on a unified 1.7M-episode robot corpus, then post-trains with the same alignment and state dropout. The auxiliary branch is dropped at inference.
- read: full (text supplied in the request; the arXiv URL was not fetched separately, and I did not check it against the source directly)
- key numbers: RoboTwin 2.0 Clean2Random 72.3% vs 46.0% for pi0.5 and 62.6% for Spatial Forcing (Table 3). Table 6 ablation at full data: 72.3% with alignment in both stages, 63.2% pre-training only, 57.1% post-training only, 48.2% neither. Real-world average 83.8% vs 59.8% for pi0.5.
- code/weights: GitHub link stated (https://github.com/OpenHelix-Team/Spatial-Forcing/tree/master/SLA) and a project page. No weights release is stated in the text.
- practical: LOW
- why: The core trick (training-only alignment head, dropped at inference) is cheap to borrow, but it only applies if you are training a VLA, and the continual pre-training run needs 48 H100s for about 110 hours. The ablations are single-seed on RoboTwin, and the 83.8% real-world result rests on 50 object instances per cell. The idea that spatial alignment during training costs nothing at inference is worth noting for any future VLA fine-tuning, but it doesn't change any design decision in your current stack.

### 1. Meta² (2611.05139)
- what: Offline, it learns a frozen textual "Meta-Skill" from A/B/C rollout contrasts (no evolver / evolver guided by the Meta-Skill / evolver with privileged verifier info), then at test time an evolver uses it to make task-local KEEP/EVOLVE harness edits at checkpoints, with each run reset to the seed harness.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL was given for the paper itself, only the arXiv id and project page https://meta-square.github.io/ listed in the text)
- key numbers: Terminal-Bench 2.1 with GPT-5.6-Terra 81.00% vs. NexAU seed 66.33% and best baseline Meta-Harness 73.33% (mean@5, 60 test tasks). DeepSWE 1.1 44.44% vs. seed 34.67%, Meta-Harness 37.33%. Ablation: task-agent-only 66.33 → online evolver without knowledge 74.67 → contrastive Meta-Skill 81.00 on TB; resetting between tasks drops TB 81.00 → 78.33 and DeepSWE 44.44 → 39.11. Full costs: $174.91 (TB) and $367.86 (DeepSWE).
- code/weights: not stated. Only the project page is linked; no repository or Meta-Skill artifact is mentioned in the text.
- practical: MEDIUM
- why: The reusable design pattern is directly transferable to a Claude Code/Muninn harness: a frozen, small guidance file of act/hold/avoid rules that a supervisor consults at checkpoints, with edits scoped to one run. The cost to replicate is high (roughly $100–$900 per benchmark in offline and online spend, plus 29 and 38 training tasks), and the authors' own evaluation rests on single-run point estimates with 60 and 75 test tasks. The gains on DeepSWE (about +9.8 points on 75 tasks, 3 repeats) are noisy, and the paper's own limitations section says the A/B/C contrasts are not causal.

### 1. CoworkOS: Scaling Agent Coworkers for Real-world Automation (2611.03178)
- what: Describes CoworkOS, a harness that splits a Main agent (strategy and acceptance) from a Coordinator runtime and delegated Subagents, adds shared document/CAD/Blender resources with revision control, persistent workspaces and Jobs, and reports a five-round automated post-training run on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL fetched, paper text only)
- key numbers: Post-training average over eight benchmarks rises 33.19 → 42.95 (+9.76) across five rounds, with no ablation isolating the harness contribution. Benchmark table: CoworkOS 55.22 Tool Use vs DSH 55.31, 57.54 Productivity vs DSH 56.13, 56.26 ML Coding vs DSH 56.14, all with one model (GLM-5.3) and single runs; no variance reported.
- code/weights: Repo github.com/RUC-NLPIR/CoworkOS and project page coworkos-ai.github.io are stated in the paper. Model weights for the post-trained Qwen checkpoint are not stated.
- practical: MEDIUM
- why: The reusable parts are concrete: the Subagent evidence-contract and bounded-wait/fallback pattern for async delegation, the optimistic-revision rule for shared artifacts, and the "resume from durable state, re-inspect external state before repeating" recovery rule, all of which map onto Muninn's delegation and memory design. The headline benchmark margins over DSH are small, come from one backbone with no error bars, and the harness is not separated from the model in the comparisons, so I would not treat the competitiveness claims as evidence that the architecture is what drives the results.
